attribution.note: Marcus wrote this sentence himself in his own Substack post. He is not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: The drafter's version keeps 'usual', the link to the announcement, and 'within hours'. It is a checkable statement about reports that appeared after the launch.

contract.note: Reading the claim as several concrete public reports of obvious Gemini 3 mistakes, appearing within hours of the announcement, is an ordinary plain reading. It also fairly allows early-access reports as long as the version caveat is disclosed.

evidence.note: Semafor's launch coverage is timestamped 11:00 a.m. EST on Nov 18. This means the announcement happened at or before that time, which gives the starting point for counting hours.
Firsthand Gemini 3 Pro test. The transcript puts the meeting's end at about 1h04m, but it actually ended at about 3h31m. That is a plain error, and e4 shows the report was public on launch day.

Karpathy reports Gemini 3 insisting it was not 2025 and calling real articles fake, an embarrassing result. The displayed time has no timezone, but the post ID puts it at about 18:51 UTC, consistent with e4. He suspected he was given an earlier version.

Techmeme archive of the site at 5:00 PM ET on Nov 18. Per the packet it contains both reports, so both were circulating no more than about six hours after the 11 a.m. coverage. The quoted excerpt shows only the archive timestamp, not the reports themselves.

reviews.rationale: Two firsthand public reports of obvious Gemini 3 mistakes, a wrong transcript timestamp and refusing to accept the current year, were circulating by 5 PM ET on launch day, about six hours after the 11 a.m. EST coverage. Karpathy's report carries an early-version caveat, which the contract allows if disclosed. Nothing in the packet shows the reports came later or concerned another model. The word 'usual' is Marcus's own characterisation and is not separately tested.

semantics.note: Faithful to the words and keeps 'basically' and 'squandered'. The claim is a statement of fact, but 'squandered' adds a judgment that OpenAI was responsible, so scoring depends on a causal question. The contract handles that through its causal axis.

contract.note: Reading 'squandered' as wasting an advantage through one's own decisions or execution is the ordinary meaning, not a stretch. Requiring evidence of that responsibility, and treating catch-up alone as unresolved rather than mixed, is fair. Because the result depends on this reading of 'squandered', the interpretation flag is set to true.

evidence.note: Independent launch evaluation: Gemini 3 Pro scores 3 points above GPT-5.1 and leads 5 of 10 evals, which implies OpenAI led before. This supports the earlier OpenAI lead and Google catching up. It says nothing about whether OpenAI wasted its lead.

Google's own launch announcement, a company disclosure rather than an independent finding. It reports topping LMArena and state-of-the-art benchmark scores, which supports catch-up only. Nothing on OpenAI's decisions.

reviews.rationale: The packet supports the factual part: OpenAI held a lead before, and Google reached and passed it at launch (e5, e6). The packet's own stated gaps say no usable record shows avoidable OpenAI decisions caused the lead to be lost. Benchmark movement cannot tell OpenAI squandering a lead apart from Google simply improving. The contract assesses the claim as a whole, so it is unresolved.
